questions.stem: A trust's operations director has been asked by a governor to 'look into whether AI could help with the complaints backlog'. She has an hour and no budget, and the governor wants an answer at the next meeting. Which question does she ask Claude FIRST to turn this into something she can actually assess?

options.text: Which of these proposed uses would be most impressive to present: triage complaints, draft response letters, summarise themes for the board, or write the monthly report?
How many complaints does the trust receive, and what is the average response time?
What general guidance exists on using AI in complaint handling in the NHS and the public sector?
What would a good AI tool for complaint handling need to do, and how much would it cost to build?

questions.explanation: A vague request like this can only be assessed once it is turned into a **current-state question with a measurable baseline**. Option B does that, and it is the only option that produces evidence she can use: the volume of work, the current response time, and the shape of the queue. Everything else is either premature or off-target. Asking which use would be most impressive (option A) invites her to pick a project on presentation appeal, which is precisely how tools get adopted for the wrong reason. Asking for general guidance or a build estimate (options C and D) presumes a solution and a procurement route before anyone knows where the time actually goes. Worth noting for the meeting itself: without a baseline, any later claim of improvement is unfalsifiable, so this first step also protects her from over-claiming later.

whyWrong.A: Choosing the most impressive use case is choosing on presentability rather than on where the work is. The first question should describe the problem as it is, so that any proposed use has to justify itself against a measured baseline.
whyWrong.C: External guidance is worth reading, but it is not the first question. She does not yet know whether the bottleneck is volume, response time, quality or knowledge, and guidance cannot tell her which of those she has.
whyWrong.D: Asking what to build and what it costs assumes a solution has already been chosen, and it invites an estimate she has no basis to produce. Requirements and cost follow from understanding the work, not from browsing for tools.

questions.mindset: Turn a vague request into a measurable current state before you discuss any solution.

questions.stem: A finance director asks a business associate to assess three candidate use cases for Claude in a 60-person finance team: (1) deciding which supplier invoices to pay, (2) drafting first-pass responses to routine supplier queries, and (3) summarising month-end variance commentary. She wants to start with the one that gives the quickest safe win. Which assessment is MOST sound?

options.text: Start with whichever is easiest to demonstrate in a demo, since a successful demo is what secures the budget.
Start with deciding which invoices to pay, because it happens every day and would save the most time.

Start with drafting routine supplier-query replies: the volume is high, the work is bounded, there is already a person reviewing and sending each reply, and an error is recoverable before it reaches anyone.
Start with month-end commentary, because commentary takes longest to write and therefore offers the biggest saving.

questions.explanation: A good first use case is judged on **volume, boundedness, existing human oversight and reversibility** — not on hours saved or demo impact. Option A is the only candidate that scores well on all four: routine queries arrive in volume, the task is well defined, a person already reviews and sends each reply, and a wrong reply is corrected before a supplier sees it. That combination means the team learns from the pilot at low risk. Option D is the one use case where a wrong output is a payment decision, which is not where a first attempt belongs. Option B confuses duration with value: the commentary is genuinely harder to get right, and 'biggest saving' ignores how much rework a weak draft creates. Option C optimises for the approval meeting rather than for the work.

whyWrong.B: Frequency measures volume, not suitability. Deciding which invoices to pay moves a control decision to a tool that cannot be accountable for it, and a mistake here reaches suppliers as a payment error.
whyWrong.D: Long tasks are not automatically good candidates. Commentary requires accurate figures and defensible reasoning, which makes it a poor first pilot precisely because errors are harder to detect and the work happens only a handful of times a quarter.
whyWrong.A: Choosing the demo-friendly option picks on presentability rather than on where the team can learn safely. A convincing demonstration is not evidence that the workflow will hold up in production with 60 people relying on it.

questions.mindset: Pick the first use case on volume, boundedness, existing oversight and reversibility — not on hours saved or demo appeal.

questions.stem: A council is redesigning its permit application process. Interview notes show three groups with different priorities: businesses want a decision in five days, residents want the most conditions possible on a permit, and enforcement officers want the most evidence they can legally require. A colleague suggests asking Claude to 'combine the requirements into one list'. Which TWO approaches would work better? Choose TWO.

options.text: Have Claude list the requirements each group stated, then identify which requirements genuinely conflict, what each group is really protecting, and which conflicts are resolvable by sequencing or by stage.
Record, against each requirement, whether it comes from an interview, from a written council policy or from Claude's own suggestion, so the team can see what is confirmed and what is unverified.
Ask Claude to produce a weighted list where the most-mentioned requirements come first, then adopt that order.
Ask Claude to draft the permit policy itself, using its knowledge of how comparable councils write theirs.
Produce two alternative combined requirement lists and let the group pick the one they prefer at the meeting.

questions.explanation: Conflicting stakeholder priorities are a **design problem to be surfaced, not averaged**, and these two options are the ones that produce something a council can actually adopt. Option A does the intellectual work: it separates the stated positions from the interests behind them, which is usually where the resolution lives — speed and thoroughness can often be reconciled by deciding at which stage a condition is applied rather than by trading one away. It also identifies which conflicts are genuine, so time is not spent negotiating the resolvable ones. Option B provides **provenance**, which is what makes the resulting list usable: an interview statement, a written policy requirement and a model suggestion have very different standing in a document that officers will enforce. The merged list destroys exactly that distinction.

whyWrong.C: A frequency ranking is not a resolution and not a decision rule. How often something was said reflects who was interviewed and how the conversation was framed, and it produces a list that appears objective while answering none of the conflicts.
whyWrong.D: Handing the drafting to Claude transfers a decision about what the council will permit to a system with no knowledge of the local policy and no accountability. Its general knowledge of comparable councils is not a source of authority for this council's requirements.
whyWrong.E: Two combined lists is not a resolution, it is the same averaging done twice. Offering the group a choice of merged documents relocates the negotiation to the meeting without recording the conflicts or where each requirement came from.

questions.mindset: Surface conflicts and record provenance separately — never merge stakeholder positions into one list and never let frequency stand in for a decision.

questions.stem: An operations manager wants Claude to monitor the shared support inbox overnight and reply to routine enquiries automatically, without a person reading them. Her manager asks you, a business associate, what you would tell her. Which response is MOST appropriate?

options.text: That this is a good candidate because the enquiries are routine and overnight cover would remove a real service gap.
That her plan does not currently let her do this, so she should assume it cannot be done, and look for other use cases instead.

To check her organisation's policy and what her workspace actually supports, and then to help her design the nearest thing that is achievable: a drafted reply for a person to check and send, with the queue prioritised overnight so nothing waits until morning.
That she should proceed with a small pilot of automatic replies to the ten most common enquiries, and expand once she is satisfied.

questions.explanation: The honest answer is **neither a yes nor a flat no, and the difference matters**. A chat workspace does not act on its own or send anything unattended, so the fully automatic version is not something she can switch on — but 'therefore give up' is also wrong, because there is usually a nearby achievable design. Option C does the work: confirm the policy and what is actually available rather than assuming, then design the nearest thing that works within her role — drafting replies for a person to check, plus overnight queue prioritisation so the genuine service gap is still addressed. Option D is the dangerous one, because a pilot that appears to work is how an unreviewed outward-facing workflow gets scaled.

whyWrong.A: Genuine operational merit does not make a use case achievable. Judging only on value leads to plans built on capabilities she does not have, and the gap is discovered late rather than in a conversation.
whyWrong.B: Concluding it is impossible without checking understates both her plan and her role. Plenty of value comes from preparation and drafting work, and she would abandon a real improvement on a technicality.
whyWrong.D: Automatic replies to customers are outward-facing and hard to recall. A pilot that is small does not make the risk small — the errors land in inboxes and are often only discovered when a customer complains.

questions.mindset: When a use case exceeds what the workspace can do, check and design the nearest achievable version instead of guessing.

questions.stem: A clinic group has written requirements for an AI-assisted appointment reminder process, and several of them cannot be tested: 'improve patient engagement', 'give a better experience', 'handle reminders professionally'. The project lead wants requirements the team can build and test against. Which TWO changes would do MOST to make them usable? Choose TWO.

options.text: Rewrite each vague requirement as an observable behaviour with a measure attached — for example, 'first reminder sent within two hours of booking', 'no appointment missed because of a reminder error' — so a test can pass or fail.
Mark each requirement as confirmed by a named policy or data source, or as an assumption to be validated, so the team knows what it may build on and what it must test first.
Add a target percentage improvement to each requirement, so the team has a number to aim at.
Rank the requirements by importance, so the most important ones are built first.
Ask Claude to rewrite the requirements in its own clearer wording, since its phrasing is usually more precise.

questions.explanation: A requirement is only useful if it can **fail**, and these two changes are what make that possible. Option A turns aspirations into observable behaviour with a measure, which is exactly what lets a build team know it is done and lets a pilot produce evidence rather than impressions — note that 'no appointment missed because of a reminder error' is a pass-or-fail criterion, whereas 'improve patient engagement' cannot fail at all. Option B adds the second missing dimension: **standing**. Some requirements come from a documented standard and can be built on; others are guesses about how patients will respond, and building on those produces rework. Together they give the team a specification and a risk list. Option C is the tempting non-answer — attaching a percentage to an unmeasurable behaviour adds the appearance of rigour without changing what can be tested.

whyWrong.C: A number attached to something unobservable is not a target, it is a decoration. 'Improve engagement by 20%' still leaves open what counts as engagement and what the current figure is, so nobody can say whether the build succeeded.
whyWrong.D: Prioritising untestable requirements is fine once they are testable and does not make them testable. Ranking cannot tell the team whether a built feature met the requirement or whether the requirement was even the right one.
whyWrong.E: Clearer wording by the same token that produced a plausible but unsupported 'three years of audited accounts' requirement in similar projects is a poor guarantee. Rewording leaves the untestability in place and obscures who asserted each requirement.

questions.mindset: A requirement must be able to fail — make it observable and measurable, and record whether it is confirmed or assumed.

questions.stem: A charity's fundraising team has to deliver its annual appeal in nine weeks, split across a live appeal, a direct mail drop, an email sequence, a gala dinner and a schools pack. The fundraising lead asks Claude for a plan in one prompt and gets a polished week-by-week schedule. Before she takes it to the trustees, what should she have Claude do?

options.text: Produce a detailed and realistic week-by-week plan that the team can follow without further changes.
Break the plan into one section per workstream, with owners and dependencies named separately.

State the plan's assumptions explicitly — including dates, staffing, approval lead times, which appeals need board sign-off and how long that takes — and list anything it had to assume because she did not supply it.
Produce three alternative approaches with different levels of ambition, so the trustees can choose.

questions.explanation: A plan is only as trustworthy as the **assumptions underneath it**, and a polished schedule hides them. Option C makes them explicit, which is what turns a document into something a trustee can challenge — a trustee who sees 'board sign-off assumed to take two weeks' can immediately say it takes five. The instruction to list what Claude had to assume because nothing was supplied is the crucial half: those are the invented specifics that would otherwise be discovered in week three, by which point the drop has already been printed. This is the planning equivalent of asking for source sentences, and it costs one extra request. Option B improves usability without touching trustworthiness, and option A and D add polish and choice rather than evidence.

whyWrong.A: A realistic-sounding schedule is what she already has. Without knowing which parts were invented, she cannot tell whether it is realistic, only whether it reads well — and confidence in the prose is exactly what misplaced it on the trustee's desk.
whyWrong.B: Workstreams, owners and dependencies are useful structure and genuinely worth having. They do not identify the invented details, so the trustees would still be approving a plan whose contents nobody has checked.
whyWrong.D: Offering three approaches creates the appearance of deliberation without adding information. Choosing between three unverified plans multiplies the checking burden rather than reducing it.

questions.mindset: Ask for the plan's assumptions before asking for more detail — a schedule is only as real as what it assumes.

questions.stem: A service manager's team handles 900 support tickets a month, averaging 22 minutes each, with 11 people. She suspects the process is slow and wants Claude to help her 'make it faster'. She has two weeks and no way to change the underlying system. Which approach is MOST likely to produce a useful result?

options.text: Ask Claude to suggest ten changes to the ticket process that would speed it up, then pick the three easiest to implement.

Map the process as it is now, record how long each step takes for a sample of real tickets including waiting time, identify where tickets wait rather than being worked on, and only then look for improvements to the steps that dominate the total.
Ask Claude which support processes are generally inefficient and compare its answer with her team's own figures.
Ask Claude to write a target handling-time policy for the team, and adopt it as the standard.

questions.explanation: Process optimisation has one prerequisite: **knowing where the time goes**, including the time spent waiting. Option B is the only approach that establishes this before proposing changes, and the detail that matters is measuring waiting rather than just work — a process where tickets sit overnight for approval looks identical to one where agents are slow, and the two have opposite fixes. Once the time is attributed, effort goes to the step that dominates the total, which is where a fortnight of effort produces a measurable change. Options A, C and D all produce plausible recommendations without evidence about her team: A generates ideas before knowing the constraint, C imports general benchmarks instead of her own measurements, and D sets a target that both misses the diagnosis and removes the ability to see whether the change worked.

whyWrong.A: Ideas generated before measurement are guesses, and 'the three easiest to implement' is a selection rule about effort rather than effect. Some cheap changes address the step that costs 2% of the time, which is how a project delivers effort and no improvement.
whyWrong.C: General benchmarks do not describe her team, her channels or her approval rules. The figure she needs is the one produced by her own tickets, and comparing against a general average risks optimising for a process that is not hers.
whyWrong.D: Writing a target first is the wrong order of operations: it creates a number to be argued about before anyone knows whether it is achievable, and without a baseline there is no way to demonstrate whether the work achieved anything.

questions.mindset: Optimise only after you know where the time goes, including the time spent waiting.

questions.stem: A charity's income team wants to compare how it runs grant due diligence against published practice, to decide where to spend a small improvement budget next quarter. It wants to use Claude's Research feature. Its process is documented in a checklist the team maintains in a shared drive, and it will take part of the due-diligence team's time to help. Which prompt design is MOST likely to give a useful comparison?

options.text: Ask for the ten most common weaknesses in grant due diligence, and score the team against them.
Ask for an assessment of the team's checklist, and take the suggested improvements as the plan.
Ask for a comprehensive review of how charities conduct grant due diligence worldwide, without reference to our own process.

Give the team's own checklist, state the decision this research supports — which part of due diligence to improve first — and ask for published practice to be compared against it, with the source and date for each practice, and for the report to say clearly where published practice does not apply to a charity of their size or funding mix.

questions.explanation: A comparison needs **both sides present**, and only option D puts them in the same analysis. The rest are worth noting: the checklist is not just context, it is the half of the comparison that makes the published half actionable, and asking Claude to assess the checklist alone (option B) produces generic improvement suggestions that will already be on the team's list. Option D also does three things that make the output usable for a budget decision — it anchors the work in the decision being made, it requires **a source and date per practice**, and it asks explicitly where published practice does not transfer. That last clause is the difference between a research report and a plan, because a small charity's due diligence will legitimately differ from the benchmark set, and without that caveat the team either adopts the wrong practice or dismisses the whole report.

whyWrong.C: A worldwide review with no reference to the team's own process is a literature summary. It cannot tell the team which part of its due diligence to change, which is the only reason to commission the work.
whyWrong.A: A list of common weaknesses is generic guidance, and scoring the team against weaknesses nobody selected for their circumstances produces a ranking with no logic behind it. It also gives no sense of which weakness costs them most.
whyWrong.B: Asking Claude to assess the checklist treats a model as an auditor of an internal control. Its suggestions will be plausible and general, and the team has no basis to judge whether any of them fit its funders' requirements.

questions.mindset: Benchmarks only help when compared against your own documented process, and only if the report says where they do not transfer.

questions.stem: A services company analyses its support process with Claude and receives a well-reasoned recommendation to move routine account queries to a self-service portal, with an estimate of a 45% reduction in contact volume. The recommendation is genuinely attractive and the operations director is keen. What is the MOST important thing to check before this is adopted?

options.text: Whether the change moves effort onto customers rather than removing it — particularly for the least confident and least digital users — and whether service levels for those customers would be protected and monitored.
Whether the portal can be built in-house within six months.
Whether competitors have already implemented self-service, so the company is not falling behind.
Whether the 45% figure is one of the range published in the analysis, and what assumptions it depends on.

questions.explanation: Every efficiency recommendation hides a **distribution question**, and this one has a specific and well-documented failure mode: work does not disappear, it moves to the people least able to absorb it. A 45% reduction in contact volume achieved by adding a portal step is a real reduction in the company's workload and a real increase in customers' — and for a customer with a disability, limited connectivity, low digital confidence or a complex problem, it can mean being excluded rather than served. That is a service-design and equality question before it is an efficiency one, so it belongs at the point of adoption. Options A and C are ordinary due diligence, and worth doing, but neither would have caught this problem; option A is competitive context, not a justification.

whyWrong.D: Interrogating the headline figure is sensible due diligence and should be done. But the figure being well-founded would not make the change good for customers, so this check alone would lead her to approve something that transfers effort outward.
whyWrong.B: Buildability is a real constraint, but it is the wrong question to lead with and it does not address the consequence for customers. Six months of feasibility work on a change that excludes some customers is effort spent in the wrong direction.
whyWrong.C: Competitor behaviour is context, not a reason. Matching competitors is a weak form of justification, and it says nothing about whether the change suits this organisation's customers or meets its obligations to them.

questions.mindset: Ask where the effort went, not just how much was saved — improvements that move work onto customers need equity checks.

questions.stem: A marketing agency has one 12-week campaign to deliver across four workstreams — website, email, paid media and partner co-marketing — with three people, one of whom is on leave for six weeks, and a fixed launch date. Claude has produced an ambitious plan with all four workstreams running in parallel from week one. Which TWO actions MOST improve the plan? Choose TWO.

options.text: Have Claude state the plan's resource and capacity assumptions explicitly, including who is actually available in each week, so the parallel assumptions can be checked against reality.
Ask for the critical path with dependencies and single points of failure named, so the workstreams that actually gate the launch date are visible.
Ask for the plan to be written with more detail on each week, so the team can see exactly what to do.
Ask Claude to rank the four workstreams by importance, and plan the most important one in detail.
Ask for a shorter plan, since a 12-week campaign does not need more than a page.

questions.explanation: The plan's central claim is that **four workstreams can run in parallel with three people, one absent for six weeks**, and that claim is currently invisible. Option A surfaces it by forcing the capacity assumptions into the open, where a manager can check them against who is actually in the room — which is how a plan built on ideal staffing gets corrected before the client sees it. Option B adds the other thing a launch plan needs: which work actually gates the date. Most rework in this situation comes from treating four parallel streams as equally important, when two of them are downstream of the other two. Note that both options target the plan's **structure and premises**; the detail-oriented request in option C produces a more readable version of the same infeasible plan.

whyWrong.C: More detail per week makes an infeasible plan more legible, not more feasible. It is a common failure mode: the polish increases confidence while the staffing assumption stays exactly as wrong.
whyWrong.D: Ranking the workstreams does not reveal that the staffing does not exist, and 'most important' is a judgement the team and client should make rather than one inferred from whatever the descriptions emphasise.
whyWrong.E: Length is not the issue; the plan is too long or too short depending on what the team needs to execute it. Cutting it to a page would remove the detail that makes the dependencies visible, which is the opposite of what she needs.

questions.mindset: Check the plan's capacity assumptions and find its critical path before you judge its detail.

questions.stem: A museum wants to build a small tool that tells visitors which of today's sessions suit a two-hour visit with a young child. She has four weeks before the pilot. What is the BEST way to start?

options.text: Build the smallest version that tests the riskiest assumption — that her timetable genuinely contains enough combinations to give a useful answer — using real timetables and a handful of example visits, before investing in the interface.
Design the interface first, so visitors see something polished at the pilot, and fit the timetable logic into it afterwards.
Ask Claude to build the full tool in one go, then correct whatever does not work during the pilot.
Write the requirements in detail first, including every field the tool will eventually need, then begin building.

questions.explanation: In a short timeline, the most valuable thing to do first is **test the assumption that could end the project**. Option A identifies it precisely — that the timetable contains enough viable combinations — and it is a real risk: if only a handful of session pairs work, the tool has nothing to offer and no interface will rescue it. Building the smallest version that answers that question first means a failed assumption costs a week rather than four, and the example visits are genuine test cases from her own data. Option B optimises for how the pilot looks on the day, which is a presentation decision taken before the substance is known; option C front-loads all the risk into a single build with no feedback; option D is requirements work that cannot be completed meaningfully until the data has been examined.

whyWrong.B: Polish first is a common instinct and usually backwards. If the timetable cannot produce useful combinations, the interface has nothing to present, and the four weeks have been spent on the part that mattered least.
whyWrong.C: Building everything at once means every assumption is tested at the same moment, at the end, with no cheap early signal about which one is wrong. That is the slowest way to find out.
whyWrong.D: Detailed requirements before looking at the data tend to be requirements for a tool nobody can yet describe accurately. The timetable is what determines what the tool needs to do, so it should be looked at first.

questions.mindset: Test the assumption that could end the project before investing in the interface.

questions.stem: A clinic manager built an interactive tool that helps reception staff estimate appointment wait times from a table of slots and lengths. After two weeks of use, staff ask for three more fields and a different layout. She is about to send all four changes in one message and then re-test. What is the BEST way to iterate?

options.text: Send all four changes in one message, since batching them is more efficient and staff are waiting.
Rebuild the tool from scratch using staff feedback, since accumulated small changes often make a build messy.
Ask Claude to explain how it calculated the estimate, so she can check the reasoning before changing anything.

Make one change at a time and re-run the same set of real appointment examples after each one, so she can tell which change fixed or broke what — and keep the cases that exposed problems as the standing test set.

questions.explanation: Iteration on a working build is an **attribution problem**, and option D is the only option that solves it. Four changes sent together produce a version that is better in three ways and worse in one, with no way to find the culprit — and the regression is the one that matters, because staff have stopped trusting a figure that was wrong last week. One change at a time against a **fixed set of real examples** turns each change into a test. Retaining the cases that exposed problems is the detail that compounds: the test set grows with every incident, so the tool gets harder to break in the places that already broke. Option C is a reasonable diagnostic and can be part of this, but understanding the calculation is not a substitute for measuring the effect of a change.

whyWrong.C: Understanding the logic can reveal a mistake, but it cannot tell her whether adding three fields or changing the layout fixed a problem. Staff reports that the estimate was wrong are about outputs, and those need output tests.
whyWrong.A: Batching is efficient for the person typing and expensive for the person debugging. It is the direct cause of the unattributable regression she is about to discover when reception stops trusting the tool.
whyWrong.B: Rebuilding discards the working version, the accumulated knowledge and the test set — the three assets that make iteration cheap. Messiness is a reason to test, not to start again.

questions.mindset: Change one thing at a time against a fixed set of real cases, and keep every case that ever broke.

questions.stem: A charity's fundraising manager has built a Claude-assisted tool that estimates whether a grant application will reach its target. She is going on leave for two weeks and a colleague will maintain it. She has 30 minutes to hand it over. What SHOULD she include?

options.text: The prompt she used, the data it expects and its format, the decisions it is not allowed to make, the known limitations, and how to change each of those things.
An export of the tool as a file, so the colleague can work on it without using Claude.
A short summary of what the tool does and what it saves, so the colleague understands the point of it.
A note that the tool's estimates should not be relied on, in case anyone treats the output as definitive.

questions.explanation: A handover has one job: **let someone else change the thing safely without you there**, and that takes a different set of information from a summary. Option A covers the four things a maintainer needs and a reader does not: the inputs and their expected format, the boundaries (what the tool must not decide), the limitations that are known to exist so they are not rediscovered as mysteries, and where to change each of these. The limits and the prohibited decisions are the most valuable items in that list, because they are the ones that are invisible in the output and unrecoverable once forgotten. Option B confuses sharing a finished document with maintaining a working tool; option C helps someone who wants to understand it rather than change it; option D states a caveat without telling the colleague anything actionable.

whyWrong.B: Exporting a file is the wrong direction for a tool that is meant to be iterated in Claude, and it removes the conversation context where the design decisions live. If the colleague genuinely needs to work outside Claude, that is a conversation to have, not a one-line export.
whyWrong.C: A description of purpose is helpful to a stakeholder and close to useless for a maintainer. Nothing in it tells the colleague what to feed the tool or which of its outputs were deliberate design decisions.
whyWrong.D: A general warning does not tell a maintainer where the tool fails, and it gives them no way to tell a failure from correct behaviour. Recording the specific known limitations is what makes the caveat actionable.

questions.mindset: A handover needs inputs, boundaries, limitations and change instructions — not a summary of purpose.

questions.stem: A logistics team's dashboard works well. The operations director sees it and asks for a module that scores each depot on a five-star scale, because 'it would look better in the board pack'. Nobody has said which measure should produce the score, and the depot managers affected will see it. The developer asks what to tell her. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Build it as a visual element, since the board pack is the reason it was requested and presentation is the actual requirement.
Say it will be built next sprint, so the director does not take the idea to the executive team herself.
Build it using the measures already on the dashboard, so it is at least consistent with what the depot managers see today.

Go back to the requester, restate the decision the module is meant to support, and ask what a depot's score would change — and if it changes nothing, decline it and record why, since a summary rating affects how depot managers are judged.

questions.explanation: A feature request that cannot be traced to a decision is where good design discipline earns its keep. Option D does the two things that matter: it **forces the purpose into the open** — if nobody can say what a five-star score would change, then it is decoration, and decoration on an operations dashboard becomes a performance signal the moment it appears in a board pack. And it recognises the second-order effect: a composite rating attached to depots affects how people are assessed and how they are spoken about, which is a consequential judgement made by an arithmetic formula nobody specified. Recording the decision not to build it means the next person to ask gets a rationale rather than starting the argument again. Note that option C is the most dangerous, because reusing existing measures looks sensible and silently invents a weighting.

whyWrong.A: Presentation value is a reason someone liked it, not a reason to build it. A decorative module becomes load-bearing the moment it appears in a board pack, because people make decisions from what is measured.
whyWrong.B: Promising it without resolving the question creates two problems at once: an expectation that has not been tested, and an escalation to a bigger audience before the team knows whether the feature makes sense.
whyWrong.C: Reusing existing measures avoids inventing new data but still invents the important part — the weighting and the thresholds that turn measures into a rating. The score would look objective while being an unexamined judgement about depot managers.

questions.mindset: If you cannot say what a feature would change, it is decoration — and decoration on a dashboard becomes a judgement about people.

questions.stem: A housing association's repairs team handles about 2,000 work orders a month. Each arrives with a free-text description from the tenant, an address, and photographs. Staff currently read every description and code it, which takes most of an hour per order. Which integration is MOST appropriate to start with, and in what role?

options.text: Use Claude to draft a suggested trade, priority and job description from the tenant's text and photos, with the sources shown, so the coordinator confirms or corrects it — a preparation step in front of a decision a person still makes.
Ask Claude to write standard job descriptions for each trade once, so the coordinator copies the right one rather than writing one.
Ask Claude to summarise the tenant's description into a single sentence for the coordinator to read, and code the trade as before.
Ask Claude to decide which trade is required and to dispatch the engineer automatically, removing the coordinator step.

questions.explanation: This is the **prepare-then-decide** pattern, and option C places Claude on the right side of the line. The reading and drafting work — turning free text and photos into a proposed trade, priority and job description — is high-volume, well defined, and checkable by someone who knows the job. Showing the sources means the coordinator can see why a suggestion was made rather than taking it on trust, which is what makes confirmation fast. Crucially, the decision and the accountability for it stay human. Option B is the tempting prize and the wrong prize: dispatch decisions have safety and cost consequences, and the errors are invisible once an engineer is on the wrong job. Option D reduces writing but not the reading that dominates the hour. Option A saves reading time but leaves the coding decision exactly where the risk is.

whyWrong.D: Automatic dispatch removes the only check between a text description and a visit to a tenant's home, with the wrong trade meaning a wasted visit and a complaint. It is also the change least likely to be reversed once it starts.
whyWrong.B: Standard descriptions are worth having but they do not address the dominant cost, which is the coordinator reading and interpreting 2,000 descriptions. Writing the job description was never the bottleneck.
whyWrong.C: Summarising to one sentence saves reading but leaves the coding judgement untouched, which is where the consequential errors are. If the code is wrong the work is dispatched wrongly no matter how briefly the description was.

questions.mindset: Put Claude on the preparation side of the line and leave the decision with a person who is accountable for it.

questions.stem: A council's revenues team has 14 people and a large backlog of routine query correspondence. Their manager wants to 'bring Claude into the process' but has not said where. Which starting point is MOST sound?

options.text: Pick the step that is high in volume, low in consequence, and already has a person checking the output — drafting routine replies is a typical candidate.
Start with the step people find most tedious, even if nobody checks it, because enthusiasm matters for adoption.
Start with the step nearest the end of the process, so mistakes are caught before anyone is affected.
Redesign the whole correspondence process first, then decide where Claude fits into the redesigned version.

questions.explanation: A first integration should be chosen on three properties at once: **volume**, so the saving is worth the change; **low consequence**, so a mistake is caught before it reaches a resident; and an **existing human check**, so the design already includes the control rather than relying on people to remember it. Drafting routine replies scores on all three, which is why it recurs as the right answer in this kind of question. The other options each optimise for something that is not the point. Tenacity and boredom are worth taking seriously as a guide to where work is heavy, but they say nothing about consequence or oversight. Redesigning before piloting is the sequencing error that ends most rollouts: the team learns nothing from a small test and then argues about a large change.

whyWrong.B: Adoption is a real concern and it is not what this choice is about. A high-volume step nobody checks is exactly how a first attempt produces a visible error in a resident's inbox and a lasting loss of trust.
whyWrong.C: Being near the end is useful when mistakes are genuinely outward-facing, but it is not a criterion in itself. A step nobody checks is risky regardless of where in the process it sits, and low-consequence steps are safer wherever they are.
whyWrong.D: Redesign-first spends the organisation's patience and political capital before anyone has evidence that the tool works at all. A small pilot generates the evidence that makes a redesign arguable.

questions.mindset: Start where volume is high, consequences are low and a human check already exists.

questions.stem: A university has Claude drafting scholarship appeals letters, which then go to a senior officer to sign. Recently the officer has begun forwarding letters without reading them, on the basis that 'the wording is always right'. Two letters last month misstated the student's circumstances. Which TWO changes would MOST protect the workflow? Choose TWO.

options.text: State in the workflow that Claude prepares the draft and the named officer decides and signs, so the decision and its consequences stay with an accountable person.
Require every letter to be checked against the student's file rather than read for fluency, and treat a misstatement as a process failure to be reviewed rather than an individual lapse.
Require two people to check every letter before it is sent, so the risk is halved.
Ask Claude to check each draft against the student's file before the officer sees it, so the officer can rely on it.
Have Claude produce three alternative phrasings for each letter and send the officer the shortest one, since brevity reduces the chance of an error surviving a read.

questions.explanation: The workflow has failed in a specific and recognisable way: **the check has been replaced by a signature**, and reading for fluency cannot detect a misstatement because the misstatement reads fluently too. Option A restores the boundary between preparing and deciding, so the person who signs is the person who decided. Option B specifies what the check should actually compare against — the student's file, the source of truth — rather than the letter's own readability, and it treats the two errors as information about the process, which is what will stop a third occurrence. Notice what option D gets wrong: it asks the component that produced the error to verify its own output against the source, which is the weakest form of checking available and would not have caught either error.

whyWrong.C: Two readers of fluent prose will miss the same thing, because the failure is not carelessness but the wrong test. Doubling the reviews doubles the time without making the check capable of finding this class of error.
whyWrong.D: Asking the drafting step to check itself against the source sounds rigorous and is not: it is the same process performing the same kind of task, with no independent comparison. A misstatement is exactly what such a check is prone to accepting, since it is internally plausible.
whyWrong.E: Brevity does not reduce the chance of a misstatement surviving review, and picking the shortest wording hands a consequential decision to a length metric. The error in both letters was a false statement about a student, and no phrasing choice protects against that.

questions.mindset: A signature is not a check — verify against the source of truth, and keep the decision with the accountable person.

questions.stem: A customer-service director has run a six-week pilot in which Claude drafted replies to about 900 enquiries, and her team says accuracy is 'around 95%'. Her director wants to quote that figure in a board paper on service quality. What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.text: Quote the figure as the pilot measured it, and note that it came from a six-week internal pilot with about 900 cases.

State what 'accurate' meant, how it was judged, by whom and on what basis, and give the figure with those conditions attached — or, if the pilot cannot support a number, report the categories of error that did occur instead.
Round the figure down to 90%, which is more defensible than a precise-sounding figure from a pilot.
Decline to quote any figure, since pilot results should not go into board papers.

questions.explanation: A percentage without a **definition and a denominator** is not evidence, it is a persuasive shape. 'Accurate' could mean factually correct, acceptable to send, or correct on first generation — and those produce very different numbers from the same pilot. Option B requires her to state the definition, the basis of judgement and who judged, which is what makes the figure meaningful and what protects her when someone asks what it actually covers. The offer of error categories rather than a number, when the pilot cannot support one, is often stronger still: it is specific, credible and demonstrates that the team was paying attention. Option A attaches caveats that do not repair the measurement. Option C adjusts the figure without fixing what was measured. Option D over-corrects — pilot evidence properly described is exactly what belongs in a board paper.

whyWrong.A: Attaching a duration and a case count to an undefined term does not repair it. If 'accurate' meant 'acceptable to send', the figure describes the reviewers' judgement rather than the tool's reliability, and the board will read it as the latter.
whyWrong.C: Rounding down is a presentational choice about a number whose meaning is still unresolved. It looks more modest while leaving the original measurement problem untouched.
whyWrong.D: Avoiding the board paper entirely discards evidence the board needs. A properly described pilot result is the appropriate thing to escalate; refusing to report it makes the pilot look like it produced nothing.

questions.mindset: Never quote a percentage without its definition, denominator, judge and period — or report error categories instead.

questions.stem: A newly promoted team leader asks Claude to write performance feedback for each of her eight reports from a list of achievements. She is enthusiastic, and two colleagues have already tried it and found the drafts 'brutal but accurate'. What is the MOST useful thing her manager can tell her?

options.text: That she should avoid it entirely, because anything said to a colleague about their performance must be written by a manager unaided.
That she is using it well, since colleagues confirm the drafts are accurate.

That it is well suited to structuring and phrasing written feedback so it is specific and well expressed, and well suited to organising the achievements into a coherent document — and that it should not be used to form or express a judgement about a person, because that judgement is hers to make, explain and defend.
That she should check every draft carefully against the achievements list, since accuracy is the only thing that matters here.

questions.explanation: The honest guidance is **a clear boundary between drafting and judging**, and option A draws it in a way she can act on. Claude genuinely is good at the mechanical part: turning a list of achievements into coherent, specific, well-phrased writing. Where it does not belong is forming and expressing an assessment of a person — because that judgement has to be owned, explained in a conversation, and defended later, none of which a draft can do. That is not an argument against the tool; it is an argument about which part of the task can be supported. Note that 'brutal but accurate' describes drafts the manager approved, which tells you the register is following her input, and it is worth saying so. Option B's framing has it backwards: accuracy is not the only thing that matters in feedback about a person.

whyWrong.B: Accurate and appropriate are different tests, and the one that matters here is appropriateness. Feedback about a person is read as a judgement by the person receiving it, and 'accurate' says nothing about whether it is fair, evidenced or deliverable in a conversation.
whyWrong.D: Checking against the achievements list is necessary and nowhere near sufficient. It does not address whether the judgement is fair, whether the tone is appropriate to the individual, or whether she can stand behind each word in the follow-up meeting.
whyWrong.A: This rejects the useful half and keeps only the prohibition. The result is a manager who hand-writes everything and gains nothing, when the drafting help is real and the boundary is the actual issue.

questions.mindset: Use it for structure and phrasing; never let it form the judgement about a person.

questions.stem: After a successful four-month pilot, a retail group's operations director wants to extend a Claude-assisted returns workflow from one warehouse to all nine. The pilot showed a clear time saving and the team is enthusiastic. Her own team notes that the review step has quietly become a formality for routine cases. Which TWO conditions should she set BEFORE scaling? Choose TWO.

options.text: Confirm the improvement against a measured baseline, sustained over a defined period, so the business case is evidenced rather than asserted.

Fix the review rules before rollout — including what must be checked, by whom, and what happens when a check finds a problem — and make sure the routine cases are actually being checked rather than waved through.
Require two people to check every return decision at every warehouse before scaling, so no single error can occur.
Roll out to two warehouses first and review after a month, so the rest of the business can see the results before committing.
Tell the nine warehouse managers the pilot results and let each decide how much review their team still needs, since they know their own operation.

questions.explanation: Scaling is where pilot weaknesses become organisation-wide, and the weakness in this case is already visible: **the control has decayed**. Option B addresses that directly, and the reason it matters more at scale is arithmetic — a check that is waved through 60% of the time in one warehouse becomes tens of thousands of unchecked decisions across nine, and the pilot's good numbers stop describing anything. It also specifies what happens when a check fails, which is the part that determines whether the control is real. Option A is the other condition, and it is about defensibility rather than enthusiasm: the saving needs a measured baseline and a sustained period, because a four-month pilot with a mid-project change of process is not a clean measurement. The other options substitute effort for rigour, or distribute the decision to people who were not part of the pilot.

whyWrong.C: Double-checking every decision sounds safe and is disproportionate: it removes the time saving that justified the pilot and will be quietly abandoned. The purpose of a review rule is to target the cases where errors are consequential, which is what the pilot's own data can now identify.
whyWrong.D: A staged rollout is sensible sequencing, but it inherits the pilot's control problem rather than fixing it, and one month is too short to reveal the slow errors this kind of workflow produces. It also delays rather than conditions the decision.
whyWrong.E: Handing the decision to managers who were not part of the pilot means the review standard is set locally and inconsistently, and each team will choose the least demanding option in a rollout where the sponsor has signalled that review is not the priority.

questions.mindset: Before scaling, evidence the improvement against a baseline and fix the review rules the pilot let decay.
